_about: Teaching text for Module 6 (molecular dynamics). Check the science before use with students.

approaches.text: A binding assay in the laboratory

scenarios.text: You have a docked pose of a drug and want to know whether it stays in the pocket over 100 ns.
scenarios.why: MD follows the atoms over time. Docking gives one frozen pose and cannot say whether it survives motion.

scenarios.text: You need a quick ranking of 50,000 compounds against one pocket.
scenarios.why: Docking is fast enough for large libraries. MD costs hours or days per compound.

scenarios.text: No structure of your protein exists, but a relative with 55% identity has one.
scenarios.why: Build a model from the relative first. MD needs a starting structure.

scenarios.text: You need the real binding strength of your best hit for a paper.
scenarios.why: Computer estimates are rough. A binding assay gives the measured value.

steps.text: Prepare the protein and ligand (add hydrogens, choose protonation states, fix missing atoms)
steps.why: The simulation needs every atom, and the charges of residues such as histidine decide the forces.

steps.text: Choose a force field and make parameters for the ligand
steps.why: The force field defines every force. A drug is usually not in the standard library, so it needs its own parameters.

steps.text: Place the complex in a box and fill it with water
steps.why: Proteins work in water. Without it the structure collapses or behaves unrealistically.

steps.text: Add ions to neutralise the charge (and reach a salt concentration)
steps.why: A box with net charge gives wrong electrostatics. Ions are placed after the water so that they replace water molecules.
Placing atoms creates clashes and huge forces. Minimising removes them before any motion starts, so the run does not explode.

steps.text: Equilibrate at constant volume and temperature (NVT)
steps.why: The system is heated slowly to the target temperature, for example 300 K, with the volume fixed.

steps.text: Equilibrate at constant pressure and temperature (NPT)
steps.why: The box size adjusts so that the density is right, for example at 1 bar.
This is the part you analyse, for example 100 ns. It starts only after the system is equilibrated.

steps.text: Analyse the trajectory (RMSD, RMSF, hydrogen bonds, energies)
steps.why: The raw trajectory is millions of numbers. The standard graphs and tables turn them into evidence.

claims.text: In this simulation, the pose stayed (or did not stay) in the pocket for 100 ns. This is one run and needs repeats and experimental testing.
claims.why: This says what the data show and how far they can be trusted. One run starts from one set of velocities.

claims.text: The simulation proves the drug binds COX-2 with the MM-GBSA energy shown.
claims.why: MM-GBSA is a rough end-point estimate that ranks well but is not an accurate binding energy, and a simulation cannot prove binding.

claims.text: A stable RMSD under 2 Å means the drug is a good drug.
claims.why: Stability of a pose says nothing about absorption, safety or potency. The 2 Å figure is a guide, not a rule.

next.text: Repeat the simulation with different starting velocities, to see whether the result is reproducible.
Run for longer or from other docked poses to check that the conclusion holds.
Test the prediction in the laboratory, for example with a binding assay or a mutation of a key residue.
Check the key hydrogen bonds and contacts against the crystal structure and the literature.
Report the MM-GBSA value as the true binding energy.
Stop here: a single stable 100 ns run proves the mechanism.
